title: Sunari: ornaments, family learning and changing work
description: Regional Sunari histories through ornament making, family learning and the changing markets of Odisha.
author: Ahimanikya Satapathy
lead: How does a community history emerge from the objects people make? Sunari accounts in Odisha lead into workshops, households and markets. They also raise a necessary question: when several communities practise the same craft, what can the craft itself tell us about identity?

sections.title: A regional name and its work

paragraphs.text: The Bhadrak District Gazetteer uses the name Sunari Bania for makers of gold and silver ornaments, including human and animal figurines. It also describes goldsmiths moving into agriculture. The passage gives no count or precise date for that change, but it preserves an important distinction: an inherited community identity can outlast a particular livelihood.
paragraphs.locator: Printed39/PDF55, Bania subsection; occupational-change scope qualified

paragraphs.text: The account belongs to Bhadrak. Its terminology cannot make every use of Bania across India equivalent, or identify the community of someone simply because they make jewellery. Names need their local histories as much as objects do.

The Census survey of traditional crafts, published in 1967, offers a striking example from Tarbha. It lists Sunari among several communities practising silverwork. Kansaris had learned the craft from traditional silversmiths; Meher weavers followed, and others entered later. The report does not identify those early teachers specifically as Sunari.

The survey counted 309 workshops in 1962, falling to 241 after closures and moves elsewhere. These totals cover the industry, not Sunari households alone. Women knitted silver-thread guinchis or cleaned ornaments during finishing. Here, the evidence describes a network of learned skills and household labour across community boundaries. Calling every worker a hereditary Sunari silversmith would erase the very movement the study recorded. The finishing work matters to this history: a workshop count alone cannot show everyone whose hands contributed to an ornament.
paragraphs.locator: Printed164–165/PDF178–179, paragraphs20 and following; industry-wide scope

paragraphs.text: In reporting published in August 2025, Niroj Ranjan Misra describes artisan families around Kotpad, most identified as Sunari, making ornaments for Bhotara customers. Pinku Sorabu learned from his father. He describes working with his mother Subarna, wife Droupadi and sister Girija: the named maker is part of a household’s labour.
paragraphs.locator: Body paragraphs beginning For over two decades; In villages like; With the help

paragraphs.text: Their materials include brass, bronze and copper. Pinku sells at Kotpad’s Tuesday market; the report also follows makers to markets in neighbouring Chhattisgarh. Customers include people beyond the original Bhotara clientele. Pinku attributes declining returns to inexpensive fashionable jewellery and asks for better market access. These are dated observations and testimony from particular families, not a measure of every Sunari household’s circumstances today.
paragraphs.locator: Body paragraphs on materials, weekly markets and Pinku’s testimony

sections.title: What the evidence can tell us

paragraphs.text: Gajapati’s district industries account likewise remembers Bania and Sunari makers fashioning gold and silver ornaments by hand with small equipment. This brief regional description reinforces the connection with skilled work, but supplies neither a community founding date nor a complete history of settlement.
paragraphs.locator: Old Time Industries, paragraph mentioning Bania and Sunaries

paragraphs.text: These records explain particular livelihoods, relationships and changes. None establishes a single founder or moment when the Sunari community was created. A fuller history would need locally grounded family accounts and dated records of settlement and service. The evidence already available gives us something more specific than an origin formula: people learning, making, changing work and finding customers.
